danish.title: Femtende bog (1812–13) — Kapitel 6
paragraphs: Den femte november var den første dag af det, man kalder Slaget ved Krasnoje. Hen mod aften — efter megen strid og mange fejl begået af generaler, der ikke gik til deres rette pladser, og efter at adjudanter var blevet sendt rundt med kontraordrer — da det var blevet klart, at fjenden overalt var på flugt, og at der ikke kunne og ikke ville komme noget slag, forlod Kutuzov Krasnoje og drog til Dobroje, hvortil hans hovedkvarter var blevet overflyttet den dag.

Dagen var klar og frostskarp. Kutuzov red til Dobroje på sin lille, buttede hvide hest, fulgt af en enorm stab af utilfredse generaler, der hviskede indbyrdes bag hans ryg. Langs hele vejen stod grupper af franske fanger, taget den dag — syv tusind i alt — og søgte at varme sig ved lejrbåle. Nær Dobroje stod en vældig flok af lasede fanger, der summede af snak og var svøbt og forbundet i hvad de havde kunnet finde, langs vejen ved siden af en lang række udspændte franske kanoner. Da den øverstkommanderende nærmede sig, forstummede snakken, og alle øjne rettede sig mod Kutuzov, der i hvid kasket med rødt bånd og en vatteret frakke, som bulede ud over hans runde skuldre, langsomt bevægede sig langs vejen på sin hvide hest. En af generalerne rapporterede til ham, hvor kanonerne og fangerne var blevet taget.

Kutuzov virkede optaget og lyttede ikke til, hvad generalen sagde. Han kneb øjnene sammen med et utilfreds udtryk, mens han opmærksomt og ufravendt betragtede disse fanger, der frembød et særligt ynkværdigt syn. De fleste var vansiret af forfrysninger i næse og kinder, og næsten alle havde røde, opsvulmede og betændte øjne.

En gruppe franskmænd stod tæt ved vejen, og to af dem — den ene med ansigtet dækket af sår — flåede et stykke råt kød fra hinanden med hænderne. Der var noget frygteligt og dyrisk i det flygtende blik, de kastede på rytterne, og i det ondsindede udtryk, hvormed soldaten med sårene straks vendte sig bort fra Kutuzov og fortsatte med, hvad han var i gang med.

Kutuzov så længe og indtrængende på de to soldater. Han rynkede ansigtet, kneb øjnene sammen og svajede eftertænksomt med hovedet. Et andet sted lagde han mærke til en russisk soldat, der leende klappede en franskmand på skulderen og sagde noget til ham i en venskabelig tone, og Kutuzov svajede med samme udtryk atter med hovedet.

»Hvad sagde De?« spurgte han generalen, der fortsatte sin rapport og henledte den øverstkommanderendes opmærksomhed på nogle standarter, taget fra franskmændene, der stod foran Preobrasjensk-regimentet.
»Ah, standarterne!« sagde Kutuzov, tilsyneladende med besvær rivende sig løs fra de tanker, der optog ham.
Han så sig fraværende omkring. Tusinder af øjne stirrede på ham fra alle sider og ventede et ord fra ham.

Han standsede foran Preobrasjensk-regimentet, sukkede dybt og lukkede øjnene. En i hans følge gav tegn til de soldater, der bar standarterne, om at træde frem og omringe den øverstkommanderende. Kutuzov tav i nogle sekunder og begyndte så, tydeligt modstræbende underkastende sig den pligt, hans stilling pålagde ham, at hæve hovedet og tale. En skare officerer omringede ham. Han så opmærksomt rundt på officerskredsen og genkendte flere af dem.

»Jeg takker jer alle!« sagde han, henvendt til soldaterne og derpå atter til officererne. I stilheden omkring ham hørtes hans langsomt udtalte ord tydeligt. »Jeg takker jer alle for jeres hårde og trofaste tjeneste. Sejren er fuldstændig, og Rusland vil ikke glemme jer. Ære være jer!«
Han holdt inde og så sig omkring.

»Sænk den, sænk den!« sagde han til en soldat, der tilfældigt havde sænket den franske ørn, han holdt, foran Preobrasjensk-regimentets standarter. »Sænk den, ned med den! Hurra, kammerater!« tilføjede han med en rask bevægelse af hagen, henvendt til soldaterne.
»Hur-r-ra!« brølede tusinder af stemmer.
Mens soldaterne råbte, lænede Kutuzov sig frem i sadlen og bøjede hovedet, og hans øje lyste op med et mildt og tilsyneladende ironisk glimt.

»I ser, brødre...« sagde han, da råbene var forstummet... og pludselig forandrede hans stemme og hele ansigtsudtryk sig. Det var ikke længere den øverstkommanderende, der talte, men en ganske almindelig gammel mand, der ville fortælle sine kammerater noget vigtigt.
Der opstod en bevægelse i officersflokken og i soldaternes rækker, da de rykkede tættere for bedre at høre, hvad han ville sige.

»I ser, brødre, jeg ved godt, det er hårdt for jer, men det kan ikke være anderledes! Hold ud, det varer ikke længe nu! Vi vinker farvel til vores gæster, og så hviler vi os. Tsaren vil ikke glemme jeres tjeneste. Det er hårdt for jer, men I er dog hjemme, mens de — I kan se, hvad det er kommet til med dem,« sagde han og pegede på fangerne. »Værre stillet end vores fattigste tiggere. Mens de var stærke, sparede vi os ikke, men nu kan vi endda have medynk med dem. De er også mennesker. Har jeg ikke ret, kammerater?«

Han så sig omkring, og i de rette, ærbødige, undrende blikke, der var rettet mod ham, læste han sympati med det, han havde sagt. Hans ansigt blev lysere og lysere med et gammelt menneskes milde smil, der trak mundvigene og øjenkrogene sammen i en klynge af rynker. Han holdt inde og sænkede hovedet som i forvirring.
»Men hvem bad dem om at komme? Godt nok til de blodige skurke!« udbrød han pludselig og hævede hovedet.
Og idet han svingede sin ridepisk, red han af sted i galop for første gang under hele felttoget og efterlod de brudte rækker af soldater, der jublende lo og råbte hurra.

Kutuzovs ord blev næppe forstået af tropperne. Ingen kunne have gentaget feltmarskallens tale, der begyndte højtideligt og derpå gik over i en gammel mands ligefremme snak; men den inderlige ærlighed i den tale, følelsen af majestætisk triumf forenet med medynk med fjenden og bevidsthed om vores sags retfærdighed, netop udtrykt gennem den gamle mands godmodige eder, blev ikke blot forstået, men lå i enhver soldats sjæl og fandt udtryk i deres jublende og vedvarende råb. Da en af generalerne bagefter henvendte sig til Kutuzov og spurgte, om han ønskede sin karet sendt efter, kom Kutuzov uventet til at hulke — tydeligvis dybt bevæget.

english.title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter 6
paragraphs: November fifth was the first day of what is called the battle of Krasnoe. Toward evening—after much arguing and many mistakes by generals who went to the wrong places, after adjutants had been sent racing about with counter-orders—when it became clear that the enemy was in full flight everywhere and that there could be no battle, Kutuzov left Krasnoe and went to Dobroe, where his headquarters had been transferred that day.

The day was clear and frosty. Kutuzov rode to Dobroe on his plump little white horse, followed by an enormous retinue of discontented generals who whispered among themselves behind his back. All along the road, groups of French prisoners captured that day—there were seven thousand of them—crowded around campfires to warm themselves. Near Dobroe, an immense crowd of tattered prisoners, buzzing with talk and wrapped and bandaged in whatever they could find, stood in the road beside a long row of unharnessed French guns. At the approach of the commander in chief, the buzz of talk ceased and all eyes turned to Kutuzov, who wore a white cap with a red band and a padded overcoat that bulged on his round shoulders as he moved slowly along the road on his white horse. One of the generals was reporting where the guns and prisoners had been captured.

Kutuzov seemed distracted and wasn't listening. He squinted with a dissatisfied expression as he studied the prisoners, who presented an especially wretched sight. Most of them were disfigured by frostbitten noses and cheeks, and nearly all had red, swollen, and festering eyes.

One group of Frenchmen stood close to the road, and two of them—one with his face covered in sores—were tearing at a piece of raw flesh with their hands. There was something horrible and animal-like in the fleeting glance they cast at the riders and in the hostile expression with which the soldier with the sores immediately turned away and went back to what he was doing.

Kutuzov looked long and hard at these two soldiers. He puckered his face, squinted, and pensively nodded his head. At another spot, he noticed a Russian soldier laughingly patting a Frenchman on the shoulder and saying something to him in a friendly way, and Kutuzov nodded his head again with the same expression.

"What were you saying?" he asked the general, who was continuing his report and directing the commander in chief's attention to some captured French standards standing before the Preobrazhensky regiment.
"Ah, the standards!" said Kutuzov, clearly pulling himself back with difficulty from the thoughts that preoccupied him.
He looked around absently. Thousands of eyes were watching him from all sides, waiting for a word from him.

He stopped in front of the Preobrazhensky regiment, sighed deeply, and closed his eyes. Someone on his staff beckoned to the soldiers carrying the standards to come forward and surround the commander in chief. Kutuzov was silent for several seconds, then, submitting with obvious reluctance to the duty imposed by his position, raised his head and began to speak. A crowd of officers gathered around him. He looked carefully at the circle of officers, recognizing several of them.

"I thank you all!" he said, addressing the soldiers and then the officers again. In the stillness around him, his slowly spoken words were clearly audible. "I thank you all for your hard and faithful service. The victory is complete, and Russia will not forget you! Honor to you forever."
He paused and looked around.

"Lower its head, lower it!" he said to a soldier who had accidentally lowered the French eagle he was holding in front of the Preobrazhensky standards. "Lower, lower, that's it. Hurrah, lads!" he added, with a quick motion of his chin.
"Hur-r-rah!" roared thousands of voices.
While the soldiers were shouting, Kutuzov leaned forward in his saddle and bowed his head, and his eye lit up with a mild and seemingly ironic gleam.

"You see, brothers..." he said when the shouts had died away... and all at once his voice and the expression on his face changed. It was no longer the commander in chief speaking but an ordinary old man who wanted to tell his comrades something very important.
A stir ran through the crowd of officers and the soldiers' ranks as they pressed forward to hear better what he was going to say.

"You see, brothers, I know it's hard for you, but it can't be helped! Bear up—it won't be long now! We'll see our visitors off and then we'll rest. The Tsar won't forget your service. It's hard for you, but still you're at home, while they—you see what they've come to," he said, pointing at the prisoners. "Worse off than our poorest beggars. While they were strong, we didn't spare ourselves, but now we can even pity them. They're human beings too. Isn't that right, lads?"

He looked around, and in the direct, respectful, wondering gazes fixed on him, he read agreement with what he had said. His face grew brighter and brighter with an old man's gentle smile, drawing the corners of his lips and eyes into a web of wrinkles. He stopped speaking and bowed his head as if in thought.
"But then again, who asked them to come here? Serves them right, the bloody bastards!" he suddenly cried, raising his head.
And flourishing his whip, he rode off at a gallop for the first time during the entire campaign, leaving behind the broken ranks of soldiers who were laughing joyfully and shouting "Hurrah!"

Kutuzov's actual words were barely understood by the troops. No one could have repeated the field marshal's speech, which began solemnly and ended as an old man's simple, heartfelt talk. But the genuine sincerity of that speech, the feeling of triumphant majesty combined with pity for the enemy and an awareness of the justice of their cause—expressed so perfectly by that old man's good-natured final outburst—was not merely understood but lived in the soul of every soldier and found expression in their joyous, prolonged cheering. Afterward, when one of the generals asked Kutuzov whether he wanted his carriage sent for, Kutuzov unexpectedly gave a sob in his reply, clearly deeply moved.
